title: Natural shifted augmentation fiber of an exact four-term row
statement:
Let $\mathcal C$ be a site small relative to the module universe and $S$ a sheaf of commutative rings. Let $A,B,C,D$ be sheaves of $S$-modules [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category] and suppose
$$0\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow{a}B\xrightarrow{d}C\xrightarrow{q}D\longrightarrow0$$
is exact. In the cochain, cone and shift conventions of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], let $P=[B\xrightarrow d C]$ in degrees $-1,0$, let $\epsilon:P\to D[0]$ have degree-zero component $q$, and put $F=\operatorname{Cone}(\epsilon)[-1]$. Then $F$ is canonically the complex $[B\xrightarrow d C\xrightarrow{-q}D]$ in degrees $-1,0,1$. The map $i:A[1]\to F$ with degree $-1$ coordinate $a$ and zero other coordinates is a quasi-isomorphism, hence specifies an isomorphism $A[1]\xrightarrow{\sim}F$ in $D(\operatorname{Mod}(S))$. Given another exact row $0\to A'\xrightarrow{a'}B'\xrightarrow{d'}C'\xrightarrow{q'}D'\to0$ and $S$-linear maps $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$ to the first row with $\beta a'=a\alpha$, $\gamma d'=d\beta$ and $\delta q'=q\gamma$, the square of augmentations induces the shifted cone chain map $r:F'\to F$ with coordinates $(\beta,\gamma,\delta)$ in degrees $-1,0,1$, and the equality $r\circ i'=i\circ\alpha[1]$ holds as chain maps. These specified isomorphisms are therefore natural for every such commuting exact-row diagram.

proof.text: Work in the abelian category $\operatorname{Mod}(S)$; the smallness hypothesis permits this. Exactness gives $da=0$ and $qd=0$, so $\epsilon$ is a chain map. The cone formula gives $\operatorname{Cone}(\epsilon)^{-2}=B$, $\operatorname{Cone}(\epsilon)^{-1}=C$, $\operatorname{Cone}(\epsilon)^0=D$, with differentials $-d,q$. The shift $[-1]$ moves these to degrees $-1,0,1$ and negates the differentials. Thus the canonical zero-summand identifications give $F=[B\xrightarrow d C\xrightarrow{-q}D]$, as asserted.

proof.text: The proposed $i$ is a chain map because $da=0$. Directly from $H^r=\ker(d^r)/\operatorname{im}(d^{r-1})$, its only possibly nonzero target cohomology objects are $H^{-1}(F)=\ker d$, $H^0(F)=\ker q/\operatorname{im}d=0$, and $H^1(F)=\operatorname{coker}q=0$. Changing $q$ to $-q$ changes neither its kernel nor its image. Exactness at $A$ and $B$ makes $a:A\to\ker d$ an isomorphism: a section of $\ker d$ locally lifts to $A$ by exactness, and the local lifts are unique since $a$ is monic, so they glue to a unique preimage. Hence $H^{-1}(i)$ is this isomorphism. In all other degrees source and target cohomology vanish. Thus $i$ is a quasi-isomorphism by definition, and localization sends it to the specified isomorphism $Q(i):A[1]\xrightarrow{\sim}F$.

source.place: Tag 0115, Definition homology-definition-quasi-isomorphism-cochain; direct kernel/image calculation in the given exact row; derived localization as in def-weil-abstract-derived-category

proof.text: For the given row diagram, let $p:P^{\prime}\to P$ have components $\beta,\gamma$. Its chain-map equation is $\gamma d^{\prime}=d\beta$; moreover $\delta\epsilon^{\prime}=\epsilon p$ is precisely $\delta q^{\prime}=q\gamma$. On the cone in degree $k$, take the block diagonal map $\delta^k\oplus p^{k+1}$ on $D^{\prime}[0]^k\oplus P^{\prime\,k+1}$. Multiplying the cone differential matrices on either side gives equal diagonal blocks by the chain-map equations, and equal upper-right blocks by the augmentation equation. It is consequently a cone chain map. Shifting it by $[-1]$ does not change its components, so under step 1 it is $r=(\beta,\gamma,\delta)$. Equivalently its two differential equations are $\gamma d^{\prime}=d\beta$ and $\delta(-q^{\prime})=(-q)\gamma$.

source.place: Tag 014E, Definition derived-definition-cone, block matrix formula; homology.tex Tag 011G, shifted morphism components; direct calculation for a strictly commuting square

proof.text: In degree $-1$, the two composites $ri^{\prime}$ and $i\alpha[1]$ are $\beta a^{\prime}$ and $a\alpha$, equal by hypothesis. In every other degree their source is zero, so the components agree. Thus $ri^{\prime}=i\alpha[1]$ as chain maps. Applying $Q$ gives $Q(r)Q(i^{\prime})=Q(i)Q(\alpha[1])$. The $Q(i)$ are isomorphisms by step 2, so this is exactly their asserted naturality. The coordinate construction of $r$ sends identity row diagrams to identities and composes by coordinate composition; hence it defines the stated natural family for all the row diagrams in the statement.
